title: Chapman
author: Sam Alamu
desc: Equal parts orange and lemon-lime soda over ice in a dimpled beer mug, with a couple of capfuls of blackcurrant cordial and a few drops of Angostura.
longDesc: Chapman is a Nigerian invention with an unusually well-documented origin: it was crafted in the 1960s by Sam Alamutu, a hotelier and manager at Nigerian Hotels, for his wife, who preferred soft drinks to alcohol — and it was first served publicly at the Ikoyi Hotel and the Ikoyi Club on Lagos Island before spreading across the country. The recipe is simple and, honestly, unquantified: equal amounts of orange and lemon-lime soda over ice, a couple of capfuls of cordial, a few drops of Angostura bitters, and cucumber and citrus to garnish. The dimpled beer mug is not optional.
ingredients: Ice, to fill a dimpled beer mug
Orange soda and lemon-lime soda, in equal amounts
A couple of capfuls of cordial or squash — blackcurrant or grenadine
A few drops of Angostura bitters
steps: Fill a dimpled beer mug with ice.
Pour in equal amounts of orange soda and lemon-lime soda.
Add a couple of capfuls of cordial or squash — blackcurrant or grenadine.
Add a few drops of Angostura bitters.
Garnish with cucumber, and lemon or lime slices.
chefTips: The dimpled beer mug is the documented serving vessel and it genuinely matters to how a chapman reads — it is a tall drink served in heavy glass.
Equal parts orange and lemon-lime is the only stated ratio. Everything else is capfuls and drops.
Cucumber is not a garnish you can skip. It is what makes a chapman taste of itself rather than of mixed fizzy drinks.
A few drops of Angostura, and no more. It is there for the bitter edge and it dominates quickly.
The drink was made for a non-drinker from the start, which is worth knowing for how you frame it — it is not a mocktail version of something alcoholic.
Build it in the glass over ice rather than mixing in a jug. The layers sort themselves out as you pour.
Blackcurrant cordial is the usual choice in Nigeria; grenadine gives a redder, sweeter drink.
commonMistakes: Using only one soda rather than both.
Mixing it in a jug and losing the fizz.
Serving it without enough ice, so it goes flat and warm.
sources: Adapted from 'A Bit of the Nigerian History of Chapman', published on kitchenbutterfly.com. ATTRIBUTION FLAG, AND IT IS A REAL ONE: this page's byline came back as 'Christina Orleans', dated 16 August 2026 — NOT Ozoz Sokoh, and not even the site name that every other page on that domain carries. Two independent research passes found the site's bylines unreliable: most pages byline as 'Kitchen Butterfly' with a bulk 'Modified: June 3, 2026' stamp, and this one carried a personal name belonging to neither. The content is cited to the site with that discrepancy stated plainly rather than attributed to anyone.

DOCUMENTED PROVENANCE, as printed: Sam Alamutu, born 1933, a hotelier and manager at Nigerian Hotels, 'crafted the Chapman for his wife in the 60s because she preferred soft drinks to alcohol.' First public service, verbatim: 'After home taste tests, the first public introduction was at Ikoyi Hotel, and by extension Ikoyi club, a country club on Lagos Island. From there, it spread across the country.'

SOURCES THAT PAGE CITES: an October 2020 Business Day feature, plus a reader comment from Ms. Sola Alamutu identifying herself as Sam Alamutu's daughter. That is a first-degree family corroboration on the record, which is unusually strong for a cocktail attribution.

THE RECIPE AS GIVEN CARRIES NO QUANTITIES, and that is stated rather than filled in. As printed: ice in a dimpled beer mug; 'equal amounts of orange and lemon-lime soda'; 'a couple of capfuls of cordial or squash — blackcurrant or grenadine'; 'a few drops of Angostura bitters'; garnish of cucumber, lemon and/or lime slices.
The ONLY ratio stated anywhere is 1:1 orange to lemon-lime. 'A couple of capfuls' and 'a few drops' are not quantities and have not been converted into any.
THE DIMPLED BEER MUG is a specific and citable serving detail and is reproduced as printed.
Note also, for how the drink is framed: it was invented FOR a non-drinker, which means it is a soft drink by design rather than a non-alcoholic version of something else.
storage: Make to order. It does not keep.
healthBenefits: Cucumber and citrus add some vitamin C.
Angostura bitters contain gentian, traditionally used as a digestive.
Lower in alcohol-related harm than any cocktail, which was the point of its invention.
culturalNote: Chapman is one of very few Nigerian dishes or drinks with a named inventor, a date and a venue — Sam Alamutu, the 1960s, the Ikoyi Hotel — and a daughter on the record confirming it. It is the default party drink for anyone not drinking alcohol, served tall over ice with cucumber floating in it, and it is Lagos in a glass.
